replacement_html: Problem 4 — the simplest geometric test fails by a factor of eight. Sydney–Perth is a hard test because both endpoints sit on a fitted coordinate scaffold, so the dome can absorb error into n(r). There is a simpler geometric test the kill-shot leaves implicit: rim circumnavigation. The dome’s disc has radius 20,015 km (the ice wall), so the full rim circumference is 2π × 20,015 ≈ 125,760 km, and the Antarctic coast at ~70°S sits at r ≈ 17,791 km under the dome’s own latitude→radius mapping — a coastal circumference of order 2π × 17,791 ≈ 111,800 km. The dome author has already conceded a related geometric failure: Version 22 of the model explicitly stated: “Southern arc distances 2× too long — FAILS. Globe wins cross-equator.” V12/V13 claim to have narrowed that error using H(r); the rim test shows the underlying disc geometry was never fixed. The globe-predicted 70° S parallel circumference is 2π × 6,371 × cos(70°) = 13,691 km (∼13,700 km); recorded southern-ocean circumnavigation routes at 55–60° S log ∼20,000 km per lap — either figure is far below the dome’s ∼111,800 km prediction. That is a factor-of-eight discrepancy at the coast and a factor-of-nine at the rim. Nor does projection choice rescue this: the V12/V13 system uses an exponential H(r) mapping instead of linear AE, but any monotonic latitude-to-radius mapping that places Antarctica on or near the rim of a 20,015 km disc yields a rim circumference of ~125,760 km and a coastal circumference of the same order. The disc radius, not the projection, sets the scale. No coordinate formula, aetheric refraction, or refractive index n(r) can dissolve it: refraction bends light, but ships move through water. Hull displacement, fuel burn, and elapsed time are physical measurements immune to optical effects, and they all return ~13,700 km. This is a separate failure from the coordinate-formula debate: a factor of 8–9, not V12's 2×, and it follows from the disc radius itself rather than from any coordinate formula. A defender invoking a Finsler metric that compresses 125,760 km of "dome-Euclidean" distance into 13,700 km of fuel-burn distance is admitting the disc is a sphere in disguise on the geometric-distance test. A defender may reply that the dome remains distinctive on other tests — sun altitude, horizon dip, firmament physics — and that metric-equivalence on nautical distance need not erase those distinctions. But every one of those tests is computed against the same 20,015 km disc radius the rim test exposes; a Finsler metric that compresses 125,760 km of rim into 13,700 km of physical travel must apply to the same disc-derived geometry that fixes solar position above each latitude, horizon angle at each observer altitude, and firmament height above the disc plane. The defender's choice is metric incoherence — one rule for nautical distance, another for everything else — or metric capitulation, in which the disc's geometric distinctiveness collapses across every prediction the disc radius enters. "We win elsewhere" is not free: it costs the parameter-coherence that "we" depends on. See §7.1 for the full derivation; Test 1’s point is that the Sydney–Perth calibration succeeds in fitting one railway distance while the geometry it rides on top of fails the simplest rim test by over 700%.

anticipated_objections.objection: Bishop's ring and firmament physics are optical/atmospheric phenomena, not geometry-derived in the strict disc-radius sense — your pre-empt overreaches.
anticipated_objections.response: The objection is partially correct for optical phenomena per se (refraction, intensity), but the *positions* the dome predicts those phenomena at — angular altitude of sun at given latitude, observer-firmament geometry — all depend on the disc-radius-anchored latitude→radius mapping. The dome's own predictions page calibrates sun-altitude predictions against the same disc geometry. A metric that erases the rim's geometric content cannot then leave intact the angular geometry between observer and sun at low southern latitudes.

anticipated_objections.objection: The defender could grant the pre-empt and reply 'fine, our model is now metric-incoherent, but we have lots of physical models that mix metrics (Newtonian + GR, fluid mechanics + thermo); incoherence at this scale is acceptable.'
anticipated_objections.response: The two-metric escape is publishable but expensive: the dome would have to specify which metric applies to which prediction, justify the dividing line non-circularly, and accept that the disc-radius parameter no longer plays a unified role. Crucially, the dome's own published model does NOT currently specify a two-metric structure — invoking one to escape the rim test is a post-hoc rescue that doubles the number of free parameters and concedes the disc's original geometric content.

anticipated_objections.objection: 'Geometric distinctiveness' is rhetorical inflation — the dome is distinctive on every test we've published a verdict on, not just nautical distance.
anticipated_objections.response: Quantify distinctiveness: the dome's distinctive predictions reduce to (a) sun altitude/Bishop's ring (calibration-bound, see Part 4); (b) Polaris altitude (within Polaris's own 0.66° offset, see Test 2); (c) horizon dip (no published quantitative dome prediction). The remaining 'distinctive' surface is small. The rim test eliminates the only one of those rooted in disc geometry that's testable to ten-digit precision.

kernel_of_truth: The defender's objection has real force. The dome model does claim distinctive predictions on tests beyond geographic distance: sun altitude with Bishop's ring, Polaris altitude excess, horizon dip, firmament-dome optics. Metric-equivalence for nautical distance does not, *by itself*, demolish those other distinctions. Acknowledging this is correct adversarial play — the original 'renamed globe projection' framing overstated by treating one metric-collapse as collapse of the whole model.
why_it_doesnt_save_claim: But the disc-radius parameter is shared across every geometry-derived prediction the dome makes. The same 20,015 km that produces the 125,760 km rim circumference also fixes where on the disc each observer sits relative to the sun, the firmament, and the horizon. A Finsler metric that compresses the rim by 8× must propagate to those derived geometries — or the dome must declare metric incoherence (one rule for distance, another for everything else), which is a more expensive concession than the simple 'sphere in disguise' framing implied. Either way, the original rim-test verdict (Misleading) tightens rather than weakens: the rebuttal forces an escalating cost on the defender, not a free-pass on other tests.
